conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after baby arrives. I’m so glad you’re here.

Today I’ll be using a quick questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays between us, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you.

We’ll move through the questions one at a time, and if anything feels difficult we can pause or adjust. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

I can still laugh—just not quite as easily as before the baby. Most days I manage to smile or chuckle once or twice, especially when my partner makes a silly face at the baby, but it feels like I have to remind myself to lighten up.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes. It’s not like I never laugh—if something’s really funny I’ll still crack up—but it takes more effort than it used to. A lot of the time I’m just tired or distracted, so the little things that would’ve cracked me up before barely get a smile now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get excited about small things—like when my mom brings over a new outfit for the baby or when we have a quiet moment to watch a show together—but it’s not the same bubbly feeling I used to have. It’s more muted, like I’m happy in my head but the happy doesn’t quite reach my chest, if that makes sense.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. My partner said it’s just a phase, but I still felt like I must’ve done something wrong. It’s not every little thing, but when stuff goes sideways my mind jumps to “this is my fault.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Now and then I’ll suddenly feel on edge, like when the baby’s asleep and I’m watching his chest rise and fall—my brain jumps to “what if he stops breathing?” It’s quick, and I can usually talk myself down, but it hits me out of nowhere, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panic, but there was one night—maybe three days ago—when he wouldn’t settle and I suddenly felt my heart racing and this wave of “I can’t do this.” It passed after a few minutes once my partner took him for a bit, but in that moment I felt kind of shaky and trapped, like the walls got closer.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when the laundry piles up or he spits up right after I’ve changed him—little stuff feels heavier than it should. I usually push through, but I’ve caught myself thinking, “I can’t keep up,” even though I know it’s normal newborn chaos.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy. I do have trouble falling asleep some nights—mostly because my mind keeps running through feeding schedules or wondering if I’ll hear him cry—but it’s not like I’m lying there sobbing or feeling hopeless. I’m just restless and my brain won’t settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had a couple of weepy moments—like yesterday when I couldn’t get him to nap and I just sat on the couch with tears rolling down—but it’s not a constant thing. Mostly I feel okay, just a little flat or tired, and then out of nowhere the sadness hits for a bit and fades.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried once or twice this week, maybe a little more if you count the quick tears I blink back. It’s not an all-day thing—just short spells when I feel overwhelmed, like when he wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing him. I calm down pretty fast, but the tears still come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I get frustrated or tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavier than usual-laughing and looking forward to things take effort, worries about your baby's safety pop up unexpectedly, and you've had a few tearful, overwhelmed moments. You're still functioning and bonding with your little one, but the joy feels muted and small tasks sometimes loom large.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports a clear reduction in ability to laugh—only when something is "really funny," and even then it takes "more effort"—aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>She reports enjoyment is still present but noticeably muted, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a few times this week" and gives a specific example, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intrusive worries occurring "now and then" with recognizable anxious thoughts, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a sudden episode of intense fear, heart racing, and feeling trapped, matching 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient reports that minor stressors feel disproportionately heavy and admits recurrent thoughts of being unable to keep up, indicating reduced coping consistent with "sometimes not coping as well as usual".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the cutoff where <med>postpartum depression</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med> are likely. You describe reduced pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), frequent self-blame, sudden panic sensations, and multiple worries, meeting partial criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. While you denied hopelessness and self-harm, the combined load of depressive and anxious symptoms warrants prompt, formal evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent follow-up with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within a week
2. Request formal depression and anxiety assessment, including <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> review
3. Begin tracking mood, sleep, crying spells, and anxious episodes daily to share with your clinician
4. Explore support options: partner, family, local new-mom groups, online CBT or mindfulness programs
5. Prioritize 15-30 min of restorative time each day (shower, short walk, listening to music) while a trusted adult cares for the baby
6. Practice sleep-hygiene: dim lights, limit screens during night feeds, accept help with night-time bottles if possible
7. If distress escalates or self-harm thoughts emerge, call emergency services or your local crisis line immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [enter date]  
Source: Self-report via structured questionnaire (10-item EPDS-style) — 2–3 wk postpartum

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (reduced laughter, muted enjoyment)  
- Episodic tearfulness, “flat” mood, fleeting sadness  
- Excessive self-blame when infant fussy  
- intrusive anxious thoughts (infant breathing), one nocturnal “can’t do this” episode with racing heart  
- feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, “little stuff feels heavier”  
- initial insomnia ruminating about feeds  

Positive findings  
- Crying 1–2×/week, brief, situational  
- No sustained low mood all day  
- No anhedonia total  
- No appetite/weight items endorsed  
- No self-harm ideation ever  

Risk indicators  
- Mild-moderate anxiety with sudden somatic surge (heart racing, trapped feeling)  
- Mild depressive symptoms (tearfulness, guilt, lowered pleasure)  
- Functional impact: sleep disruption, coping strain, no impairment in basic self-/infant-care reported  

Safety  
- Denies suicidal or infanticidal ideation; no self-harm thoughts. No protective-planning needed at this time.

Screening impression  
Subthreshold mixed postpartum anxiety/depressive symptoms; does not meet provisional cutoff for major depression on this screen, but distress exceeds “baby blues” and warrants closer monitoring. Recommend routine re-screen in 1–2 weeks, psycho-education, support linkage; consider formal assessment if symptoms worsen, persist >2 weeks, or function declines.
